question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.

I am wrote a weekly column for the local newspaper.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. write a weekly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes a habitual/regular action, so the simple present tense is required, not the ungrammatical mix "am wrote" (be + V3). (नियमित क्रिया — simple present)

◦ The subject "I" takes the base verb "write" (no -s), and "weekly" here is an adjective describing the singular noun "column".

◦ Correct: I write a weekly column for the local newspaper.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "write a week" changes the meaning — "a week" is a noun of time and cannot modify "column".

• Option 3 "No improvement" is wrong because "am wrote" is a clear structural error.

• Option 4 "writes a weekly" violates subject-verb agreement; "writes" goes with he/she/it, not with "I".

NOTE

• Rule: I/We/You/They + V1; He/She/It + V1+s/es in the simple present.

• "am/is/are + V3" is passive voice and needs an object-turned-subject: "The column is written by me."

question:
Select the word segment that substitutes (replaces) the bracketed word segment correctly and completes the sentence meaningfully. Select the option 'no correction required' if the sentence is correct as given.

His temperament (disposed him to) argue readily with people.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. No correction required.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The fixed structure is "dispose somebody to do something" = to make someone inclined/likely to behave in a certain way. (प्रवृत्त करना)

◦ Here "to" is part of the infinitive "to argue", so a bare infinitive correctly follows it; and the past tense "disposed" matches the narration.

◦ Correct: His temperament disposed him to argue readily with people.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "disposed him of to" is wrong — "dispose of" means *to get rid of*, and "of to" is not a valid combination.

• Option 2 "dispose him to" wrongly uses the present tense "dispose" with a singular third-person subject ("temperament"), which would need "disposes".

• Option 3 "disposed him off to" adds a redundant "off"; "dispose off" is a common Indian-English error — the correct phrasal verb is dispose of.

NOTE

• dispose of = throw away/get rid of; disposed to = inclined to; at one's disposal = available for one's use.

• Similar structures: *incline somebody to*, *lead somebody to*, *prompt somebody to* + V1.

question:
Fill in the blank with the most appropriate option.

If it ______ been for him, nobody would even have known Monster was back!
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. hadn't.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• This is a third conditional (unreal past): If + subject + had (not) + V3, ... would have + V3. (असत्य भूतकाल की शर्त)

◦ The main clause "would ... have known" is a perfect conditional, so the if-clause must be in the past perfect — "hadn't been".

◦ "If it hadn't been for him" is a set expression meaning *but for him / without his help*.

◦ Correct: If it hadn't been for him, nobody would even have known Monster was back!

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "wasn't" cannot precede "been"; "was been" is not a valid form.

• Option 3 "couldn't" would give "couldn't been", which needs "have" — "couldn't have been".

• Option 4 "hasn't" is present perfect and clashes with the past-time reference of the sentence.

NOTE

• Conditionals: Type 1 — *If + V1, will + V1*; Type 2 — *If + V2, would + V1*; Type 3 — *If + had + V3, would have + V3*.

• Common exam phrase: "If it had not been for" = "But for" = "Had it not been for" (inversion, no "if").

question:
The statement below has been given with bracketed text. Select the option with correct Idiom for the bracketed text.

Mom said these instructions are (not understood by her) and that we should show them to Dad.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Greek to her.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "(It's all) Greek to me" means *completely incomprehensible; impossible to understand*. (समझ से परे होना)

◦ It fits the bracketed sense "not understood by her" exactly, and the sentence then explains why Dad should look at the instructions instead.

◦ Correct: Mom said these instructions are Greek to her and that we should show them to Dad.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "a smart cookie" means *a clever, quick-witted person* — the opposite of not understanding.

• Option 3 "pound the investment" is not an established English idiom and carries no such meaning.

• Option 4 "full of beans" means *lively, energetic and in high spirits*, which is unrelated to comprehension.

NOTE

• Similar idioms of confusion: at sea, in the dark, over one's head, can't make head or tail of.

• Origin: the phrase comes from Shakespeare's *Julius Caesar* — "but, for mine own part, it was Greek to me".

question:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.

Ben Essenburg is widely known / as one of the world's best portrayer / of the Everglades.
option_1: as one of the world's best portrayer
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. as one of the world's best portrayer.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The structure "one of the + superlative + plural noun" always takes a plural countable noun after it. (अनेक में से एक)

◦ "One of" implies selecting a single member from a group, so the noun must be "portrayers", not "portrayer".

◦ Correct: Ben Essenburg is widely known as one of the world's best portrayers of the Everglades.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 4 "Ben Essenburg is widely known" is correct — "be known as" takes a passive structure and "widely" properly modifies "known".

• Option 3 "of the Everglades." correctly uses "of" to link the portrayer with what is portrayed.

• Option 2 "No Error" is wrong because the singular noun after "one of the" is a definite error.

NOTE

• Related rule: *One of the + plural noun + singular verb* — "One of the boys is absent."

• Compare: known as (identity/role) vs known for (quality/achievement) — "He is known for his honesty."

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

Deceive
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Betray.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Deceive means *to deliberately mislead someone into believing something untrue; to cheat*. (धोखा देना)

◦ Betray means *to be disloyal to someone, to break their trust* — the closest match in meaning among the options.

◦ Correct: He tried to deceive (betray) his closest friend for money.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 Assist = to help or support someone (सहायता करना) — an antonym in spirit.

• Option 3 Aid = help, assistance (मदद) — again the opposite idea.

• Option 4 Release = to set free or let go (मुक्त करना) — unrelated to trickery.

NOTE

• Synonyms of deceive: dupe, delude, hoodwink, swindle, defraud, beguile.

• Antonyms of deceive: enlighten, guide, be honest with, undeceive.

question:
Select the word from the options which is similar in meaning to the bracketed word given in the sentence below.

Having begun my life in a children's home I have great (empathy) with the little ones.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Affinity.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Empathy means *the ability to understand and share the feelings of another*. (समानुभूति)

◦ Affinity means *a natural liking, closeness or fellow-feeling for someone/something* (लगाव) — it best conveys the speaker's felt connection with the children.

◦ Note the collocation in the sentence: "affinity with" the little ones, exactly like "empathy with".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 Apathy = lack of interest, concern or emotion (उदासीनता) — the direct opposite.

• Option 2 Passion = intense enthusiasm or strong emotion (जुनून) — too strong and not about shared feeling.

• Option 4 Hostility = unfriendliness, enmity (शत्रुता) — clearly opposite in sense.

NOTE

• Distinguish: sympathy = feeling *for* someone; empathy = feeling *with* someone; apathy = feeling *nothing*.

• Collocations: *affinity with/for*, *empathy with/for*, *sympathy for*.

question: Choose the sentence with no spelling error.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Take the offence of “locking on”.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Two words must be checked here: offence (British spelling; American offense) and locking. (अपराध / जकड़ना)

◦ Offence is spelt with a double ‘f’ and the ending -ence; locking is "lock" + "-ing".

◦ Correct: Take the offence of “locking on”.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 misspells "locking" as “lokcing” (letters transposed).

• Option 3 misspells "offence" as “ofence” (single ‘f’).

• Option 4 misspells it as “ofense” (single ‘f’ and wrong ending).

NOTE

• British vs American: offence/offense, defence/defense, licence (n)/license, practise (v)/practice.

• Frequently misspelt SSC words: occurrence, embarrass, harass, committee, privilege, maintenance.

question: Four words are given, out of which three words are spelt correctly. Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. EQUIPTMENT.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is EQUIPMENT — *the tools or apparatus needed for a purpose*. (उपकरण)

◦ It is formed as equip + ment; there is no ‘t’ before "-ment", even though the word is pronounced with a "p" sound only.

◦ Correct: The laboratory ordered new equipment for the students.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 INOCULATE (single ‘n’, single ‘c’) = to vaccinate against a disease (टीका लगाना) — correctly spelt.

• Option 2 MEMENTO (not "momento") = a keepsake or souvenir (स्मृति-चिह्न) — correctly spelt.

• Option 4 CEMETERY (three ‘e’s, no ‘a’) = a burial ground (कब्रिस्तान) — correctly spelt.

NOTE

• Note the double consonant in equipped/equipping but single ‘p’ in equipment.

• Other commonly misspelt pairs: argument (not arguement), judgment/judgement, acknowledgment.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Give and take
option_3: A competition where the outcome is difficult to judge or predict
option_4: It seems likely, reasonable, or typical
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Compromise, cooperation between people.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "give and take" means *mutual concession — a willingness on both sides to yield something in order to reach agreement*. (लेन-देन / आपसी समझौता)

◦ It stresses cooperation and adjustment, not conflict; it is often used about marriages, negotiations and teamwork.

◦ Correct: Every successful partnership needs a certain amount of give and take.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 describes a hostile clash — closer to idioms like *"lock horns"* or *"cross swords"*.

• Option 3 describes an unpredictable contest — that is the idiom *"a toss-up"* or *"neck and neck"*.

• Option 4 "It seems likely, reasonable, or typical" matches *"stands to reason"*, not "give and take".

NOTE

• Related idioms: meet halfway (compromise), bury the hatchet (end a quarrel), see eye to eye (agree).

• "Give and take" also works as a noun: "There was plenty of give-and-take in the discussion."

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose ‘No error’.

In order to survive, humans need to eat ascorbic acid, also known as vitamin C.
option_2: need to eat ascorbic acid, also
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. No error.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Every part of the sentence is grammatically sound, so no correction is needed. (कोई त्रुटि नहीं)

◦ "In order to survive" is a correct infinitive of purpose; the plural subject "humans" agrees with the plural verb "need".

◦ "need to eat" correctly uses "need" as a main verb followed by a to-infinitive, and "also known as" is a standard reduced relative clause (= which is also known as).

◦ Correct: In order to survive, humans need to eat ascorbic acid, also known as vitamin C.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is fine — an introductory infinitive phrase is properly set off by a comma.

• Option 2 is fine — "need" as a full verb takes "to + V1"; only as a modal (in negatives/questions) does it take the bare infinitive: "You needn't go."

• Option 3 is fine — "known as" correctly introduces an alternative name.

NOTE

• "In order to / so as to / so that" all express purpose; "in order to" + V1, "so that" + clause.

• Ascorbic acid = Vitamin C; its deficiency causes scurvy — a frequently asked static-GK link.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.

The sleeping rooms in a college or public institution
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Dormitory.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A dormitory is *a large room, or a building, containing several beds where students or inmates of an institution sleep*. (छात्रावास / शयनशाला)

◦ The word comes from Latin *dormire* = "to sleep", which makes the link to "sleeping rooms" exact.

◦ Correct: The new dormitory can accommodate two hundred students.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 Convent = a community/building where nuns live (कॉन्वेंट/मठ) — religious, not a college sleeping hall.

• Option 3 Monastery = a residence of monks (मठ) — again a religious community.

• Option 4 Arsenal = a place where weapons and ammunition are stored or made (शस्त्रागार).

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions: Hostel (lodging for students/travellers), Barrack (soldiers' quarters), Hangar (aeroplane shed), Aviary (place for birds), Granary (storehouse for grain).

question:
A sentence has been given with a blank to be filled with an appropriate option. Choose the correct alternative.

I told you not to give my number to ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. anyone.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• With a negative idea ("told you not to give") English uses any- words, not some- words. (नकारात्मक वाक्य में any)

◦ "Not ... anyone" = *no one at all*, which is exactly the intended prohibition.

◦ Correct: I told you not to give my number to anyone.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "other" is an adjective/determiner and cannot stand alone as a pronoun here; it would need "others" or "the other".

• Option 3 "someone" is used in affirmative sentences; "not ... someone" wrongly suggests one particular person is excluded.

• Option 4 "each one" refers to members of a specific known group one by one, which does not suit an open prohibition.

NOTE

• Rule: some/somebody/something → affirmatives and polite offers; any/anybody/anything → negatives, questions and conditionals.

• Exception: "some" is used in questions expecting "yes" — "Would you like some tea?"

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym to substitute the bracketed word in the given sentence.

Their humble attire did little to detract from the air of (imperious) authority they exuded, however.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Meek.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Imperious means *arrogant, domineering, expecting instant obedience*. (दबंग / अधिकारपूर्ण)

◦ Its opposite is meek — *quiet, gentle, submissive and unwilling to assert oneself* (विनम्र/दब्बू).

◦ Correct (antonym substituted): Their humble attire did little to detract from the air of meek authority they exuded, however.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 Unofficial = not authorised or formal — unrelated to the idea of a commanding manner.

• Option 3 Peremptory = insisting on immediate obedience, leaving no room for refusal — a synonym of imperious.

• Option 4 Lordly = haughty, grand, behaving like a lord — again a synonym, not an antonym.

NOTE

• Synonyms of imperious: overbearing, dictatorial, high-handed, autocratic, imperative.

• Antonyms: meek, humble, submissive, docile, deferential. Do not confuse imperious with imperial (relating to an empire).

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose ‘No error’.

Neither Ram nor his sisters are ready to play the game.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. No error.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• With "neither ... nor" (and "either ... or"), the verb agrees with the nearer subject — the proximity rule. (निकटता का नियम)

◦ The subject closest to the verb is the plural "his sisters", so the plural verb "are" is perfectly correct.

◦ Correct: Neither Ram nor his sisters are ready to play the game.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 4 "Neither Ram nor" is correct — "neither" is always paired with "nor", never with "or".

• Option 3 "his sisters are ready" is correct — plural noun with plural verb, and "ready to + V1" is the right structure.

• Option 1 "to play the game." is a correct infinitive completing "ready".

NOTE

• If the order were reversed — "Neither his sisters nor Ram is ready" — the verb would become singular.

• Also place the pronoun to match the nearer subject: "Neither the boys nor the captain has done his duty."

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The greatest source of income in India is ______ from agriculture and related industries.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. derived.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Derive means *to obtain or get something from a particular source*, and it collocates with the preposition from. (प्राप्त करना)

◦ The passive "is derived from" is the standard expression for stating where income, energy or a word originates.

◦ Correct: The greatest source of income in India is derived from agriculture and related industries.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 expressed = stated or conveyed in words (व्यक्त करना) — income is not "expressed from" a sector.

• Option 3 assumed = supposed without proof, or taken on (मान लेना) — it does not take "from" in this sense.

• Option 4 voiced = spoken aloud, made known verbally (कहना) — unrelated to a source of income.

NOTE

• Fixed collocation: derive from / derived from / derivative of; also *benefit derived from*, *pleasure derived from*.

• Similar source-verbs: stem from, spring from, originate in, arise from, emanate from.

question:
Select the most appropriate word for the given group of words.

A sacred place
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Sanctum.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A sanctum is *a holy or sacred place, especially the innermost shrine of a temple*. (पवित्र स्थान / गर्भगृह)

◦ It comes from Latin *sanctus* = "holy"; the innermost shrine is the sanctum sanctorum ("holy of holies").

◦ Correct: Only the priests may enter the sanctum of the temple.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 Relic = an object surviving from the past, often a saint's remains (अवशेष) — an object, not a place.

• Option 2 Museum = a building where objects of historical/artistic interest are displayed (संग्रहालय) — not sacred.

• Option 4 Retreat = a quiet place of withdrawal, or the act of withdrawing (एकांत स्थान) — secluded but not necessarily holy.

NOTE

• Related words: Sanctuary (a holy place / a protected area for wildlife), Shrine, Sanctify (to make holy), Sanctimonious (making a show of piety).

• Other one-word substitutions: Crypt (underground room beneath a church), Cloister (covered walk in a monastery).

question:
Fill in the blank with the most appropriate option.

It's a challenge, as you yourself said, and men find it hard to turn ______ challenges.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. down.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrasal verb "turn down" means *to reject or refuse an offer, request or challenge*. (अस्वीकार करना)

◦ The sentence says men find it hard to refuse a challenge, so "turn down challenges" is the only meaningful fit.

◦ Correct: It's a challenge, as you yourself said, and men find it hard to turn down challenges.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "turn up" means *to arrive/appear unexpectedly* or *to increase volume* — it does not take "challenges" as an object in this sense.

• Option 2 "turn below" is not an English phrasal verb at all.

• Option 4 "turn aside" means *to deflect or divert something (a blow, a question)*, which does not convey refusal of a challenge.

NOTE

• Other "turn" phrasals: turn in (submit/go to bed), turn out (prove to be), turn over (hand over), turn against (become hostile to), turn into (change into).

• Synonyms of "turn down": decline, reject, rebuff, spurn, refuse.

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

Obsession
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Dislike.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Obsession means *an idea or desire that continually preoccupies the mind; an overpowering fixation or liking*. (सनक / अत्यधिक लगाव)

◦ Its opposite is dislike — *a feeling of aversion or distaste* (नापसंदगी); where obsession is excessive attraction, dislike is rejection.

◦ Correct usage: His obsession with cricket slowly turned into a dislike for the game.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 Delusion = a false belief held despite evidence (भ्रम) — related to false thinking, not the opposite of fixation.

• Option 3 Compulsion = an irresistible urge to act (विवशता) — a synonym-like partner of obsession, not an antonym.

• Option 4 Relaxation = rest or easing of tension (विश्राम) — the opposite of tension, not of obsession.

NOTE

• Synonyms of obsession: fixation, mania, preoccupation, infatuation, fetish.

• Remember the pair obsessive-compulsive; "compulsion" is about the act, "obsession" about the thought.

question:
Select the word segment that substitutes (replaces) the bracketed word segment correctly and completes the sentence meaningfully. Select the option 'no correction required' if the sentence is correct as given.

(The shocked entrance) of so many witnesses seemed to have brought them to their senses.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The unexpected entrance.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• An entrance cannot itself be "shocked" — the participle -ed describes the feeling of a person, while an event needs a describing adjective. (भाव बनाम कारक)

◦ "Unexpected" correctly modifies the event: the witnesses' arrival was not anticipated, which is why it jolted the others to their senses.

◦ The singular "entrance" is also right — the many witnesses came in as one single act of entering, and it agrees with the singular verb "seemed".

◦ Correct: The unexpected entrance of so many witnesses seemed to have brought them to their senses.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "The shocking entrances" wrongly pluralises "entrance", breaking agreement with the singular verb "seemed".

• Option 3 "The unexpecting entrances" is doubly wrong — "unexpecting" is not standard usage and the plural again clashes with "seemed".

• Option 4 is wrong because "shocked entrance" is an incorrect adjective-noun combination.

NOTE

• Rule: -ing adjectives describe the *cause* (a boring lecture); -ed adjectives describe the *person's feeling* (a bored student).

• Compare: *shocking news* (cause) vs *shocked listeners* (feeling).

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

A submerged memory half rose in the king's (1) ______, and sank again. Around him he could hear murmurs, courtiers (2) ______ who the stranger was. He (3) ______ a councillor to lead the (4) ______ to the treasury, where each day gifts (5) ______ to the needy, but the brahmin shook off the man's hand.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. mind.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The standard collocation for a recollection surfacing is "a memory rose in his mind" — the mind is the seat of thought and memory. (मन/मस्तिष्क)

◦ The sentence already contains "memory", so repeating "memory" would be tautological; "mind" completes the image of something surfacing and sinking again.

◦ Correct: A submerged memory half rose in the king's mind, and sank again.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "presence" refers to being physically present — a memory cannot rise in someone's presence in this sense.

• Option 2 "brain" is the physical organ; ideas and memories are idiomatically said to occur in the mind, not "in the brain".

• Option 4 "memory" repeats the subject of the same clause and makes the sentence redundant.

NOTE

• Useful collocations: come to mind, bear in mind, cross one's mind, slip one's mind, at the back of one's mind.

• "Submerged" here means *buried or hidden below the surface* — hence the water imagery of "rose" and "sank".

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

A submerged memory half rose in the king's (1) ______, and sank again. Around him he could hear murmurs, courtiers (2) ______ who the stranger was. He (3) ______ a councillor to lead the (4) ______ to the treasury, where each day gifts (5) ______ to the needy, but the brahmin shook off the man's hand.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. wondering.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "courtiers ______ who the stranger was" is a reduced relative clause (= courtiers who were wondering), so a present participle (V1+ing) is required. (वर्तमान कृदंत)

◦ The phrase modifies "murmurs ... courtiers" and cannot carry a finite verb of its own without a conjunction.

◦ Correct: Around him he could hear murmurs, courtiers wondering who the stranger was.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "were wonderful" uses an adjective and destroys the sense — the courtiers are curious, not marvellous.

• Option 2 "wonder" is a bare present-tense verb that clashes with the past narrative ("could hear", "was").

• Option 3 "were wonder" is ungrammatical — "were" cannot be followed by the bare verb "wonder".

NOTE

• Participle phrases: "I saw a boy crying in the street" (= who was crying).

• "Wonder" + indirect question keeps statement word order: "I wonder who the stranger was" (not "who was the stranger").

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

A submerged memory half rose in the king's (1) ______, and sank again. Around him he could hear murmurs, courtiers (2) ______ who the stranger was. He (3) ______ a councillor to lead the (4) ______ to the treasury, where each day gifts (5) ______ to the needy, but the brahmin shook off the man's hand.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. ordered.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The structure needed is "order + object + to + V1" — *order somebody to do something*. (आदेश देना)

◦ The passage is in the past tense ("rose", "sank", "could hear", "shook off"), so the past form "ordered" maintains tense consistency.

◦ Correct: He ordered a councillor to lead the stranger to the treasury.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "controlled" is past tense but wrong in meaning — "control someone to lead" is not a valid structure.

• Option 2 "orders" is present tense and breaks the past-tense narrative.

• Option 3 "controls" is wrong on both counts — present tense and an unsuitable verb pattern.

NOTE

• Verbs taking object + to-infinitive: order, ask, tell, advise, allow, permit, request, compel, force, persuade.

• Contrast with make/let + object + bare infinitive: "He made him go", "She let him stay".

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

A submerged memory half rose in the king's (1) ______, and sank again. Around him he could hear murmurs, courtiers (2) ______ who the stranger was. He (3) ______ a councillor to lead the (4) ______ to the treasury, where each day gifts (5) ______ to the needy, but the brahmin shook off the man's hand.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. stranger.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Contextual clue: the previous clause says the courtiers were wondering "who the stranger was", so the person being led to the treasury is that same stranger. (अजनबी)

◦ Referring back to an already introduced noun with "the stranger" preserves the cohesion of the passage.

◦ Correct: He ordered a councillor to lead the stranger to the treasury.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "friend" contradicts the passage — nobody in the court even knows who the man is.

• Option 2 "sage" is never used for him in the given text; he is described only as a brahmin/stranger.

• Option 3 "businessman" has no support in the passage and clashes with his being taken to receive gifts meant for the needy.

NOTE

• In cloze tests, always hunt for lexical repetition and reference words (the, this, he) — they usually point to the answer.

• Vocabulary: stranger = an unknown person; strange = odd/unfamiliar; do not confuse with foreigner (a person from another country).

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

A submerged memory half rose in the king's (1) ______, and sank again. Around him he could hear murmurs, courtiers (2) ______ who the stranger was. He (3) ______ a councillor to lead the (4) ______ to the treasury, where each day gifts (5) ______ to the needy, but the brahmin shook off the man's hand.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. were given.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject is the plural noun "gifts", and gifts are receivers of the action, so a plural passive verb is required: *were + V3*. (कर्मवाच्य)

◦ The whole passage is in the past tense, so the past passive "were given" keeps the tense consistent.

◦ Correct: ... the treasury, where each day gifts were given to the needy.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "have been given" is present perfect passive and clashes with the past narrative.

• Option 2 "have to given" is ungrammatical — "have to" must be followed by a bare infinitive ("have to give").

• Option 4 "was given" is singular and does not agree with the plural subject "gifts".

NOTE

• Passive formula: object + be (correct tense/number) + V3 + (by agent).

• Tense-wise passive: Present — *is/are given*; Past — *was/were given*; Present Perfect — *has/have been given*; Future — *will be given*.
